```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(httptest2)
start_vignette("start")
set_redactor(function(x) {
  gsub_response(x, "index.php/api/catalog/", "")
})
```

Many statistical agencies and international organizations publish survey and
census microdata through catalogs built with the NADA software. All of these
catalogs share the same web API, so one package can search them all. nadaverse
wraps that API in a few functions that return data frames and lists.

This guide follows one example from start to finish. You will find a study in
the World Bank catalog, read its description, and look at its files and
variables. Then you will run the same search on a second catalog.

The output shown here comes from saved responses, so the guide builds without
an internet connection. When you run the code yourself, the functions call the
live catalogs.

```{r library}
library(nadaverse)
```

## Choose a catalog

Every function takes a catalog code as its first argument. `catalogs()` lists
the codes and prints a short summary. Use `show = FALSE` to get the table
without the printout.

```{r catalogs}
cats <- catalogs(show = FALSE)
cats[, c("catalog", "name")]
```

Codes are not case sensitive, so `"wb"` and `"WB"` mean the same catalog. This
guide uses `"wb"` for the World Bank and `"fao"` for the Food and Agriculture
Organization.

## Search for studies

`search_catalog()` returns one row per study. The `ps` argument sets how many
studies come back on a page.

```{r search}
res <- search_catalog(
  "wb",
  keyword = "Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey",
  ps = 5
)
head(res[, c("idno", "nation", "year_start")], 5)
```

Two columns identify a study. `id` is a number and `idno` is a text ID. Every
function that takes a study accepts either one. The table also has columns
such as `title`, which this guide leaves out to keep the output narrow.

If nothing matches, `search_catalog()` gives a warning and returns `NULL`
instead of an empty table.

## Read a study description

`metadata()` returns the full description of one study as a nested list.

```{r metadata}
study <- "ETH_2015_ESS_v03_M"
md <- metadata("wb", study)
names(md)
```

The `doc_desc` part describes the documentation itself, such as who prepared
it and when. The `study_desc` part describes the study:

```{r study-desc}
names(md$study_desc)
```

You can follow the list down to a single item with `$`, for example
`md$study_desc$title_statement`.

## List the data files

A study is usually split into several data files. `data_files()` shows them.

```{r files}
files <- data_files("wb", study)
head(files[, c("file_id", "file_name", "case_count")], 5)
```

`case_count` is the number of rows in a file. The table has more columns, such
as `var_count` (the number of variables) and `description`; the guide shows
only a few so the rows stay short. The `file_id` column is what you pass to
`data_dictionary()` to look at one file.

## Look up the variables

`data_dictionary()` lists the variables, with a name and a label for each.

```{r dictionary}
dict <- data_dictionary("wb", study)
head(dict[, c("vid", "name", "labl")], 5)
```

To see only one file, pass its ID:

```{r dictionary-file, eval = FALSE}
data_dictionary("wb", study, file_id = files$file_id[[1]])
```

Large studies have thousands of variables, so it often pays to start with one
file.

## Try another catalog

The functions work the same way on every catalog. Only the catalog code
changes.

```{r fao}
fao <- search_catalog("fao", keyword = "food insecurity", ps = 5)
head(fao[, c("idno", "nation", "year_start")], 5)
```

Column names come from each catalog's API, so a column that exists in one
catalog can be missing in another. Check `names()` before you rely on a column
in code that runs across catalogs.
